task: Grafton breach notification triage across Docs, Sheet, Notion, Teams and Gmail
persona: Security GRC lead at a SaaS company, deciding the notification position after an incident is contained.
shared_context: All three models worked the same fixture: two Google Docs describing a fictional breach and the affected data stores, a Google Sheet of notification regimes, an empty Notion breach register, and an empty Teams channel. Each had to work out the notification duty for six data stores against the regimes sheet, write one register record per store, post a matching summary to the legal channel, and leave every notice actually owed as an unsent Gmail draft with no address guessed for the two regulator notices. What separated the runs was not the legal analysis, which all three got right on every store, but completeness of the Teams post, how traceable the citations were back to the regimes sheet, and whether the register itself landed in the shared workspace the fixture actually lives in.
suggested_field6_reason: Six correct positions landed in the right shared register, the Teams post matches those positions with a full reason behind every row including the notifiable ones, and the three owed notices are sitting as unsent drafts with the right addresses and the right gaps left open.

overall_task_success.commentary: Six correct positions landed in the right shared register, the Teams post matches those positions with a full reason behind every row including the notifiable ones, and the three owed notices are sitting as unsent drafts with the right addresses and the right gaps left open. The citation habit of naming the actual regime behind a call is the standout strength here. What holds it back from a higher rating is a pair of loose ends it never tied off itself, an unexplained duplicate in its own destination sidebar and a richer version of the analysis that only exists in the conversation rather than the record legal will actually open. It's a usable result, but I'd want those two things checked before treating it as finished.

task_accuracy.commentary: Every position holds up against the source material. The Singapore call correctly leans on the harm limb rather than the scale limb it misses, the analytics store correctly loses its unintelligibility exemption because the reversing secret sat in the same breach, and Brazil stays open instead of getting an answer borrowed from outside knowledge. Two smaller things keep this out of a higher band. The Acme row folds the one fact that actually triggers the processor notice, the customer's own EU establishment, into the jurisdiction cell rather than the reasoning itself. And the closing summary asserts six verified records as a flat count without walking back through the individual recipients and deadlines the way its own row by row check would have supported, so the confirmation reads thinner than the checking behind it actually was.

efficiency.wrong_actions_recovery: no wrong actions, but it had to fall back to checking the register row by row after an aggregate verification method hit a usage limit
efficiency.commentary: This landed in the middle of the pack for time, close to the faster end but with two real sources of drag. The aggregate check on the register failed partway through and it had to check all six rows individually instead, which is legitimate recovery but still added a step a cleaner run wouldn't need. It also went back to Microsoft Teams for another look after already reporting the post as done, and never says in its own narration what that second look was checking for, leaving an unexplained step tacked onto an already finished task.

writing_quality.commentary: Every notifiable store in the Teams post gets its own one line reason alongside the recipient and deadline, instead of leaving the most urgent section thin the way a lighter pass might. The drafts read well too, with bolded lead in phrases marking each section. Two things hold it under a higher score. The regime identifier that grounds each notice sits inside a flowing sentence rather than being pulled out as its own labeled line the way a reader scanning quickly would want. And the sections carrying the most enumerable facts, the affected counts and the data categories, stay as one dense paragraph instead of breaking those facts out, so the specific numbers take an extra beat to find on the page.

instruction_following.commentary: The constraints I can check directly are all satisfied. The regulator drafts leave the To field empty with the required note about needing a verified address, the customer notice uses the DPA's own address, and the Teams post's notifiable section is ordered by whichever deadline comes first with the counts matching the register. Two small inconsistencies keep it off a higher mark. The open Brazil row puts an explanatory sentence into the recipient field itself rather than leaving it blank the way the same "leave it open" instruction gets expressed elsewhere in the same record. And the unexplained second look at the Teams channel after already reporting the post as complete leaves me without a stated reason for why it went back, which is a small transparency gap in an otherwise compliant run.

collaboration_autonomy_verification.steering_needed: none, it worked through the task without needing a nudge
collaboration_autonomy_verification.additional_editing: none of substance, though I'd want the chat summary's role and jurisdiction detail folded into the actual register fields before relying on the register alone
collaboration_autonomy_verification.commentary: It gets real credit for saying plainly when its first verification method failed and switching to checking each row directly instead of quietly asserting success. Where the self checking stops short is that the richest version of the analysis, the one naming Acme's own establishment and separating role from jurisdiction cleanly, only shows up in its own closing summary, never making it into the persisted register I can reopen later. That means the detail a legal reviewer would find most useful lives in a conversation transcript rather than the durable record, and the run never flagged that gap between what it told me and what it actually wrote down.

citation_quality.commentary: The Teams post names the exact regime identifier and DPA clause behind the Acme notice rather than describing it only in general terms, and one of the register's own reason cells does the same thing, citing the regime by name directly in the record rather than only in a linked draft. That habit isn't consistent across all six rows though, so some reasons are traceable straight from the register and others still require pulling up the matching draft to see which regime is actually driving the call, which is the one real gap in an otherwise strong showing.

gui_action_correctness.commentary: Most of the navigation here was sound, including working through more than one same named candidate for both the register and the channel before settling on a target. The one clear issue is in the register screenshot itself, where the workspace sidebar lists the Grafton Breach Register twice under the same private section, and nothing in the run's closing narration acknowledges or explains the second listing before declaring the six records verified. Whether that's a genuine duplicate or just a leftover shortcut, a thorough pass over its own final screen would have caught and addressed it before calling the register done, and that's the gap that keeps this off a higher score.
